transcript:
Meeting: Umbrage Systems - internal zero-trust & KMS checkup
Date/Time: 2026-05-21 14:00 UTC
Duration: ~58 minutes
Attendees: Jordan (Redwood AE), Mei (Redwood SE), Diego (Redwood SE), Alex (CISO), Priya (Lead DevOps), Marcus (Legal), Samir (Platform)

Summary: Quick security deep-dive for Private deployment options. Focus on network isolation, ingress/egress controls, KMS integration and rotation, audit logs and retention, and SSO/RBAC mapping. Customer leaning toward private VPC in their cloud with potential on-prem stub for inference nodes.

Topics: network peering, dedicated NATs, firewalling, KMS envelope integration, key rotation, SOC2/ISO evidentiary needs, RBAC mapping to SAML groups, audit log retention and SIEM ingestion

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Jordan: All right hey everyone thanks for joining on time, um we'll put an agenda in the chat, quick intro from our side, Mei is gonna lead the tech bits, I'll cover contracts and SOC2/ISO questions and Diego will be on KMS and ops.
[00:18] Alex: thanks Jordan, yeah glad to be here, we had a look at the quickstart, we're fairly deep in regulatory pre-checks so want to make sure architecturally this sits well.
[00:28] Priya: hi, I just want to be clear we are considering a private VPC deployment in our AWS account with a limited egress path and some on-prem inference proxies, so we need details.
[00:40] Mei: great, that matches what we've seen a lot. I'll start with high-level isolation then walk egress patterns. Quick note, sorry if I mispronounce some terms — transcript sometimes says K V cash — it's K V cache.
[00:52] [01:02] Mei: So for Private mode we offer a control plane that is either hosted or customer-managed; the inference plane can be in your VPC or connected via a dedicated peering/privatelink. You can pin models, opt for quantized variants, yada yada. The important security pieces: SAML-based SSO + Role based access control, mutual TLS between our control plane and the inference nodes, KMS integration for model keys and customer data encryption, and per-request audit logs.
[01:40] Priya: for the peering, is it VPC peering or PrivateLink? We have strict egress policies and only allow specific endpoints outbound.
[01:50] Mei: We support both. PrivateLink is preferred for strict egress because you can control the endpoint and do VPC endpoint policies; peering is fine if you want lower latency but you need to manage route tables carefully. For egress from inference nodes we do a couple options: 1) no egress — inference nodes don't need outbound internet if models are local and KMS is VPC endpoint enabled, 2) controlled egress via NAT/egress proxy — we recommend a dedicated NAT gateway per subnet and a restricted outbound whitelist.
[02:21] Alex: And how about on-prem stubs — if we put some inference hosts on prem behind our firewall and they call back over a dedicated tunnel how does the control plane reach them?
[02:33] Diego: Good question — we often use an IPsec/Direct Connect overlay, or a reverse SRV tunnel from the on-prem host to the control plane. For airgapped we provide an offline bundle, but for connected on-prem we prefer mTLS with client certs plus mutual auth to authenticate nodes. There is some chatter in docs where reverse tunnel is called "egress-only agent" — that might show up as odd wording in the transcript.
[02:58] Priya: can you elaborate on the KMS pattern — we run AWS KMS, HSM-backed. Do you wrap keys with your own KMS or can we bring our own key (BYOK)?
[03:10] Diego: You can BYOK. We support external key wrapping where you control the customer-managed key in your KMS; Redwood will call KMS via a VPC endpoint or over private network as configured. For envelope encryption we recommend using separate key keys per environment and rotating on a quarterly cadence. We can integrate with AWS KMS, GCP KMS, Azure Key Vault, and HSM via PKCS#11 for private deployments.
[03:39] Marcus: Legal question — does Redwood store plaintext user data in its control plane logs or any long-term storage? We need to map data residency and retention for SOC2 evidence.
[03:52] Jordan: short answer: for Private deployments you can opt out of log shipping to our hosted control plane; audit logs can be forwarded to your SIEM via syslog/CloudWatch Kinesis or retained locally. By default hosted mode keeps short-term logs for observability but for enterprise contracts we put in terms for retention and deletion. We'll share the specific SOC2 artifacts.
[04:14] Alex: what's 'short-term'? we need 90 days of immutable audit logs for now, with S3 archival for 7 years for compliance.
[04:24] Jordan: we can do 90 days live retention and export to S3 or your archival storage. We'll add retention options in our enterprise addendum.
[04:32] [05:00] Priya: We have an existing egress firewall that only allows outbound to three IP ranges. Does Redwood require dynamic ranges? we need stable addresses to whitelist.
[05:13] Mei: For hosted endpoints we publish stable CIDRs per region but if you want private-peering we can use static ENIs or PrivateLink endpoints that live in your account so no external whitelisting. For dedicated we can provision customer-dedicated IP pools.
[05:28] Samir: Is there a cost delta for PrivateLink vs peering? not a dealbreaker but helpful to know.
[05:34] Jordan: there's both a product delta and cloud cost — PrivateLink has per-hour endpoint costs on AWS and networking egress pricing; we can show an example sheet.
[05:41] [06:00] Diego: on RBAC and SSO mapping — we map SAML groups to Redwood roles (admin, dev, auditor). You can sync groups from Okta/AzureAD and we honor SCIM for provisioning. For on-prem local admins you can keep a fallback admin but it's opt-in.
[06:18] Marcus: will SCIM provisioning produce a proof we can provide to auditors? like logs of who was assigned admin, when?
[06:26] Mei: Yes, provisioning events are captured in audit logs. We also emit change events with actor, timestamp, and origin IP (sometimes masked if behind NAT). Those logs can be exported to your SIEM.
[06:40] Alex: How granular is the audit trail for model prompts and outputs? We can't keep PII in logs in many cases.
[06:48] Diego: We have three levels: full request/response capture for debugging (opt-in), metadata-only (request ID, model, token counts, user id), and redacted capture where you only store hashes of user inputs for traceability without storing PII. For compliance you can choose redaction or on-prem retention only.
[07:10] Priya: That redaction is important. Does the redaction happen client-side or on the inference node?
[07:17] Mei: Redaction can be performed at the inference node before logs leave your network. For hosted footprints there's also an SDK filter that can scrub fields before submission. There's some nuance — for some analytics you need token counts which are derived locally.
[07:30] [08:00] Alex: About key rotation — can we enforce our rotation windows and require node re-enrollment? We want to be sure old keys can't liven used.
[08:10] Diego: Yes, rotation is managed by you in BYOK. We support key versioning and automatic rewrap mechanisms; when a key is rotated nodes will fetch new wrapped keys and there is a re-enrollment job you can schedule. We can also provide a cert revocation list for node certs.
[08:22] [08:40] Priya: Are there any agents that phone home with metadata we should be aware of? We've seen agents that send hostnames or CPU telemetry out.
[08:49] Mei: we collect basic heartbeat info for node health, like instance ID, region, version number. If you need zero telemetry we can switch to an offline bundle with manual pushes, but you'll lose automatic patching.
[09:00] Samir: We run a Palo Alto firewall stack. Any special integration or suggested NAT rules?
[09:09] Mei: You can do application-based rules allowing specific outgoing TLS to PrivateLink endpoints. We recommend TLS 1.3, mTLS for node auth and restrict outbound to the control-plane FQDNs or endpoint IPs. For traffic between control plane and nodes use TCP keepalive and restrict by port (default 443/8443).
[09:26] [10:00] Marcus: Legal — indemnities around data leakage? if a node misconfig leads to data leaving, what's the responsibility?
[10:09] Jordan: that's contract language. Typically customer is responsible for misconfiguration; we provide operational guardrails and runbooks. For enterprise we offer managed onboarding and a higher SLA with remediation commitments. We'll hand over the sample clause.
[10:22] Alex: Could you walk through an example network diagram for PrivateLink with on-prem stubs?
[10:30] Mei: sure — I'll sketch it and follow-up with a pdf. High level: customer VPC with PrivateLink endpoint to Redwood service in the region, inference subnet with no route to internet, NAT for outbound controlled to a dedicated NAT, and an optional transit VPC for multi-account scenarios. On-prem hosts connect via Direct Connect/Transit Gateway and talk to the same PrivateLink endpoints.
[11:02] Priya: how do we handle egress for model downloads or container updates? They need to pull images at times.
[11:10] Diego: model artifacts can be pre-staged into your S3 or private registry; we support an offline image bundle for airgapped installs. For regular updates you can have a restricted egress to our artifact endpoint or mirror artifacts into your internal registry.
[11:28] [12:00] Alex: SOC2/ISO — what evidence will you give us? we need controls mapping and test results for subservice obligations.
[12:09] Jordan: we'll provide SOC2 Type II report, ISO 27001 cert if applicable, and a controls mapping matrix that shows which controls Redwood owns vs customer. We'll also give pen test summary and vulnerability cadence.
[12:30] Marcus: we need to confirm logs are tamper-evident and how chain-of-custody is preserved.
[12:38] Mei: logs can be signed and shipped to an immutable S3 bucket with object lock; we also support forwarding to an external log archive.
[12:48] [13:00] Priya: for RBAC we want a fine-grained role that allows model rollouts but not key management. is this doable?
[13:08] Diego: yes, roles are separate. We can map SAML groups to roles, and enforce separation: rollout role, admin role (keys, billing), auditor role (read-only with log access).
[13:22] Alex: One of our concerns is the bootstrap of trust—how are initial node certs provisioned?
[13:29] Mei: initial certs can be minted by your private CA and signed onto nodes, or Redwood can issue a provisional cert during onboarding that you rotate out. For high-assurance we recommend you bring your own CA.
[13:40] [14:00] Samir: about telemetry we mentioned, can we tag logs with our internal user ids and not email addresses? we don't want usernames in logs.
[14:08] Diego: you can map identity fields in the SDK to your internal identifiers; by default we try to capture minimal identity unless explicitly requested.
[14:18] [15:00] Priya: Let's talk about firewalling egress rules for the NAT — what's the minimal set of FQDNs/IPs needed for an update pull and KMS calls?
[15:27] Mei: minimal: KMS VPC endpoint IPs, Redwood artifact endpoint IPs (or your internal mirror), and control-plane PrivateLink endpoint. We'll send a static list for the region. Note: some cloud providers use dynamic IPs for storage endpoints so mirroring to S3 in your account is recommended.
[15:50] [16:00] Alex: For SIEM integration we use Splunk. How do logs ship? via forwarder?
[16:07] Mei: we can push to your Kinesis/CloudWatch; from there your Splunk forwarder can ingest. Alternatively we support fluentd/fluent-bit agents to ship logs to your SIEM.
[16:20] Marcus: On legal logs retention: we need proof that deletes occur when requested. Is there an API to delete customer-held logs?
[16:29] Jordan: For hosted we expose an API and a contractual right to delete; for private deployments you control log deletion. For hosted, deletion actions are captured in audit logs so you have proof.
[16:44] [18:00] Priya: We're also looking at throughput and latency when the inference nodes are in our AZ and models are large — will PrivateLink add noticeable latency?
[18:10] Mei: PrivateLink usually adds minimal latency compared to internet routing and avoids NAT traversal. The bigger latency drivers are model size and KV cache locality — we advise co-locating KV cache and models in same AZ and use our batching configs to hit latency SLOs.
[18:28] Samir: is there any encryption-in-flight variance for quantized models?
[18:34] Diego: no, encryption-in-flight is the same. The runtime handles quantized tensors locally; network traffic remains TLS/mTLS.
[18:44] [20:00] Alex: Performance testing — we want a baseline test inside our network. Can you provide a test harness we can run?
[20:09] Mei: yes, we'll provide a lightweight load generator and a benchmark spreadsheet to run in your environment, plus recommended configs for batching and KV cache.
[20:25] Jordan: we'll also propose a 30-day pilot with a small reserved capacity so you can measure cost/latency.
[20:34] [22:00] Priya: A few friction points: 1) our security team is strict on third-party outbound endpoints, 2) legal needs clear SLAs on data deletion, and 3) we need to see KMS rotation logs.
[22:14] Jordan: all reasonable. We'll send the SOC2 pack and a sample contract clause. For KMS logs, Diego will provide the rotation audit example.
[22:24] Diego: I'll include an example key rotation runbook and sample meta logs showing key versions and timestamps.
[22:34] [24:00] Alex: Any gotchas with transit gateway costs when we route cross-account to an ops VPC?
[24:08] Mei: there are transit costs, and cross AZ data charges. For production we often recommend a transit VPC pattern to centralize endpoints and reduce per-account endpoints. We'll put cost examples in the follow-up.
[24:22] Priya: Is there a recommended minimum subnet sizing for inference pools? We need to allocate IPs carefully.
[24:30] Diego: recommend at least /22 for medium fleets, /24 for very small tests. But if you use PrivateLink the count of ENIs matters more than IPs. We'll give a table.
[24:48] [30:00] (discussion continues with dig into runbook specifics; some cross talk; Speaker 1 interrupts occasionally)
[30:12] Jordan: quick recap before we run long: next steps are Mei to draw and send the VPC+onprem diagram, Diego to send KMS rotation and redaction docs, Jordan to send SOC2/ISO pack and pricing pilot. Samir to send current firewall rules and egress CIDRs.
[30:34] Priya: timeline wise we want a pilot start by early june if possible.
[30:40] Jordan: that's doable — we'll aim for onboarding week of June 2.
[30:46] Alex: one more — can you sign an NDA prior to sharing internal architecture?
[30:52] Jordan: yes we have a mutual NDA template, I'll attach it.
[31:00] [45:00] (longer technical aside about TTLs, cache warming patterns, and container signing; some audio garble noted as 'Speaker 1' in transcript)
[45:30] Mei: technical note on cache warming — if you bootstrap with a warm KV cache you avoid a lot of cold-start latency; we can assist with warm-up scripts.
[46:00] Samir: for node reboots do you support stateful volumes for local model cache?
[46:08] Diego: yes, we recommend local NVMe-backed volumes for cache and a pre-warm process after deploy.
[46:20] [52:00] (closing)
[52:10] Jordan: thanks everyone, we'll get these artifacts into you by Monday, 5/25. If anything else comes up reach out on the thread.
[52:22] Alex: great thanks all.
[52:30] Priya: thanks.

Action items (from transcript):
- Mei: send VPC + on-prem PrivateLink diagram and region CIDRs (due 2026-05-25)
